translation: The limitless roar of the sea didn't stop for a minute.
It rolled in long waves, intensifying and then subsiding.
The wind started to rustle in the bare trees, then fell silent, just like I did while listening to the flow of the night.
Yet it didn't leave, but stayed right there.
I knew this by the smell of wet pebbles and by barely perceptible tremor of a single plane tree leaf.
I had noticed this obstinate grey leaf earlier that day, but now at night it seemed like a tiny living creature, my only vigilant friend.
Every now and again gunshots carried over from the city within darkness.
After each shot dogs would bark for a long while.
Then far out at sea there was an intermittent dim light which shortly faded away.
He forced us to look at these things longer and more closely than we typically do, and to discover in them many qualities we had previously overlooked.
For instance, the pug-nosed yellow stone was full of small seashells tightly embedded in it.
On the broom bushes, a few flowers still remained, sitting on straight firm stems like soaked and wrinkled golden butterflies patiently waiting for the sun.
However, it rarely broke through the fog as a blurred white spot, providing neither warmth nor shade.
Underneath the lone old plane tree with lemon spots on its trunk lay leaves that seemed to be cut out from lackluster green velvet.
Ants ran one by one along an iron gate carrying their final winter stores into their subterranean granaries while beneath an anchor chain lived a timid little frog.
At night, someone on the other side of the river started to wave a lantern and shout longingly.
I went to the shore with my Uncle Ilko.
The river roared.
Water rushed over the dam like a cold waterfall.
The late, profound night shed no stars above our heads.
A wild freshness from the flooding, thawing ground blew in our faces.
All that time, someone waved their lantern on that shore and shouted but due to the noise of the river we couldn't make out any words.
When the coffin was carried out on the porch, I saw on the other side of the river an old carriage, horses untethered and tied to it, and my mother in black.
She stood motionless by the river bank.
She watched from there as they carried my father out.
Then she fell to her knees and bowed her head onto the sand.
"No," answered Grandfather.
"That's true, they didn't see each other again.
Ostap began to go blind.
He decided then to make it up to St Petersburg so that he could see her while he wasn't yet completely blind.
He reached the tsar's capital and found out that she had died, she, perhaps, couldn't bear the separation.
Ostap found her graveyard with a white marble stone, looked at it and his heart broke there was his iron rose lying on the stone.
She had willed for this rose to be place on her grave forever.
And then Ostap started lamenting and most likely died on his way or in a marketplace under a cartwheel .
Amen!"
On the opposite bank, Countess Branicka's sacred forest climbed up a slope.
The sun couldn't penetrate through the dense greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally did a solitary ray slice diagonally through the thicket, revealing to us the astounding power of vegetation.
Little birds flew into this beam like sparkling dust particles.
They chirped as they chased one another and then dove into the leaves as if into green water.
I filled a bucket with water from the pond, threw some grass into it, and waited.
The red floats remained stationary in the water.
Then one of them would begin to tremble, creating faint ripples around itself before suddenly diving or swiftly darting off to one side.
My father would hook it: the line became tense, bending the walnut rod into an arc as turmoil broke out above the misty surface of the pond.
The water scattered, oscillating lily pads as quicksilver beetles hurried away in all directions and finally from beneath surfaced a flailing golden glint.
It was impossible to discern what this was until my father hauled a heavy crucian carp onto the flattened grass.
It lay on its side, panting and flicking its fins; emanating from its scales was a remarkable smell evoking an underwater kingdom.
Yasha was timing himself.
We knew that from Sturdza Lane to Landesman's sanatorium, it was a seven-minute walk.
At the sanatorium behind high fences and iron gates, we always felt completely safe.
Especially if we didn't light incense burners.
As we walked past the gate, Yasha tripped over.
Later on, when reminiscing about the incident in Sturdza Lane, Yasha asserted that whenever you're intending to do your absolute best at something, you invariably screw up over trivia.
But in my opinion it was all due to Yasha's unbearable gait; nevertheless I kept quiet so as not to upset him.
We sneaked off down the alley.
I said we should go on the side where the gateway was, stop just short of it, listen carefully, and then quickly and silently dart past the portal.
The plan was mathematically precise in my opinion.
If there were people in the gateway, they might not see us at all.
But if we were to travel on the side opposite to that of gateways, they could spot us from a distance.

I calculated that in this latter scenario we would be exposed to danger from passing by or rather within sight of people hidden in gateways for five times longer hence five times more chances of getting noticed.
In the morning I would wake up to the hot sun beating against the white walls.
Red and yellow hollyhocks swayed by the open window.
Along with them, a nasturtium flower peeked into the room; a furry bee was nestled within it.
Frozen in place, I observed how it stubbornly backed out and extricated itself from the narrow flower.
On my ceiling ran endless streams of light, gentle waves reflected off of the river.
The river rustled right there, nearby.
